prompt: A container and a VM both run on the same physical server. What is the key architectural difference in what each actually has, kernel-wise?
choices: The VM shares the host's kernel; the container boots its own separate kernel
The container shares the host's kernel via namespaces/cgroups; the VM boots its own independent kernel on top of a hypervisor
Both share the host's kernel, but the VM uses more RAM
Neither shares the host kernel; both always boot a fresh kernel

prompt: Running `docker run --rm alpine uname -r` prints the exact same kernel version as running `uname -r` directly on the host. What does this prove?
choices: Alpine Linux happens to use the same kernel version by coincidence
Docker copied the host's kernel version string into the container's metadata
The container is not running its own kernel at all -- it is making syscalls directly to the one shared host kernel
This only happens on Linux hosts running Alpine as the base OS

prompt: After installing Docker on Ubuntu and running `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, why is this step necessary?
choices: It installs the Docker CLI binary for the first time
The Docker daemon's socket is owned by root:docker by default, so your user needs group membership to run docker commands without sudo
It downloads the nginx and alpine base images in advance
It is required only on Windows and macOS, never on Linux

prompt: You run `docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27`. What does the `-p 8080:80` flag do?
choices: Limits the container to 8080 MB of memory and 80% CPU
Maps port 8080 on the host machine to port 80 inside the container, where nginx listens
Pulls version 8080 of the image and tags it as 80
Sets the container's process priority to 8080 with a timeout of 80 seconds

prompt: What is the practical difference between `docker logs web` and `docker exec -it web /bin/bash`?
choices: They are two names for the same command
`docker logs` shows the container's past stdout/stderr output; `docker exec` opens a new interactive process (like a shell) running inside the already-running container
`docker logs` only works on stopped containers, and `docker exec` only works on running ones that were started with `-it`
`docker exec` restarts the container, while `docker logs` does not

prompt: You start three containers from the same nginx:1.27 image and write a new file inside only one of them (web1). Why can't web2 and web3 see that file?
choices: Because each container has its own private writable layer on top of the shared read-only image layers, so changes in one are invisible to the others
Because the image itself gets modified, but only web1 is allowed to read the modification
Because each container actually downloads a completely separate full copy of the image
Because docker exec always operates on a random container, not the one you named

prompt: Why does starting a 4th container from an image you've already pulled take well under a second, even if the image is hundreds of megabytes?
choices: Docker secretly runs all containers from one image as a single shared process
The read-only layers are already present on disk and get mounted (via a union filesystem like overlayfs), not copied -- only a small writable layer is newly created
Docker caches a pre-booted container in RAM at all times
Small images are always used for the 2nd and subsequent containers automatically

prompt: You run `docker run -d --name flaky busybox echo "starting up"` and then `docker ps` shows nothing running. What's the most accurate explanation?
choices: The container crashed due to a Docker installation bug

A container's lifecycle is tied to its main (PID 1) process; `echo` printed its output and exited immediately, so the container exited right after -- it needs a long-running foreground process to stay up
busybox images cannot be run detached with -d
The --name flag is incompatible with -d and silently fails the whole command
